You know, the CDC changed their guidelines to basically say six feet of social distancing is not a prerequisite. It should be done to the greatest extent practical. And that is a big change in policy. And what that means is in places where there's low COVID, It is okay and universal masking. It is okay to have kids three feet apart, as long as they're masked and you're in a place where there's very, very low COVID. I had a constructive conversation with Corey Rosenley from HSTA. I've been talking to both UPW and HGA. And I think the good news is that everybody is saying that they want to reopen in-person schools as quickly as possible. Now come the logistics. It takes the reconfiguration of physical space. it takes covid protocols new training for teachers and principals and and other school staff so if we've decided to do this and i think we have collectively although that's not a formal decision but i haven't talked to a major education or government leader who doesn't agree we should re-open the schools as soon as it's possible, then the logistics are going to be tremendously challenging. And so the kind of logical pivot point would be for us to kind of operationalize some of this stuff so that we could have spring break and then try to do in-person learning to the greatest extent possible. Now, I just got to say this. There are certain teachers who are going to be needing reasonable accommodations because of their health issues, and that's a real thing. I am suggesting that if the COVID rates stay this low or even continue on their downward trajectory, we have to be ready for the possibility that we could actually save the fourth quarter of this academic year. It'll take a lot of doing, and it'll take a lot of negotiating, and one of the conversations I had with Corey Rosinley was, look, we should do this all within the context of collective bargaining.
